                <h3>Dead Fish Swimming Upstream</h3>

              <p class="resource-description">
                This fascinating demonstration shows a dead fish swimming upstream, illustrating remarkable fluid dynamics principles. 
                The phenomenon demonstrates how passive body shapes can generate propulsive forces through interaction with fluid flow, 
                even without active propulsion mechanisms. This research connects to fundamental questions about how passive dynamics 
                and active control interact in biomechanical systems—a core theme of the AffineDrift research framework.
              </p>
              <p style="margin-top: 1rem; font-size: 0.95rem; color: var(--text-light);">
                <strong>Research Source:</strong>
                Liao, J. C., Beal, D. N., Lauder, G. V., &amp; Triantafyllou, M. S. (2003).
                Fish exploiting vortices decrease muscle activity.
                <em>Science</em>, 302(5650), 1566–1569.
                <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1088295" target="_blank" rel="noopener">https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1088295</a>
              </p>
              <p style="margin-top: 0.5rem; font-size: 0.9rem; color: var(--text-light); font-style: italic;">
                Liao et al. showed that trout can maintain position in a vortex street using near-zero muscle activity —
                the body passively exploits fluid forces to generate forward propulsion. This is a biological example
                of drift-dominated dynamics: the passive body geometry interacts with environmental forcing to produce
                coordinated motion without active control, directly analogous to the drift term in the control-affine
                golf swing model.
              </p>
